meta.author: bank-team-integrated-2
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Apply the product rule to count outfit pairs
questions.stem: A workplace report lists 4 jacket colors and 3 pant styles; how many outfits use one of each?

options.text: 12 outfits, found by multiplying 4 colors by 3 styles
7 outfits, found by adding 4 colors to 3 styles
options.misconception: adds the two counts instead of multiplying them

options.text: 4 outfits, found by using only the jacket colors
options.misconception: ignores the second independent choice entirely

options.text: 3 outfits, found by using only the pant styles
options.misconception: ignores the first independent choice entirely

questions.explanation: Each of 4 jackets pairs with each of 3 pants, so multiply to get 12. Adding counts would merge distinct categories and undercount.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of independent choices.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the sum rule to count mutually exclusive options
questions.stem: A field report offers 5 bus routes or 3 train routes, never both; a colleague claims 15 total routes.

options.text: The colleague added 5 and 3 to get 8, not 15
The colleague multiplied 5 and 3, but mutually exclusive choices add
The colleague ignored the never-both condition entirely
options.misconception: invents a condition not stated in the report

options.text: The colleague counted only the bus routes

questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive alternatives add: 5 plus 3 equals 8. Multiplying applies to independent sequential choices, not alternatives.
questions.hint: Add counts for either-or, multiply for and.

questions.learningObjective: Compute permutations allowing repeated symbols
questions.stem: A workplace code uses 4 symbols, each position any of 4 symbols; how many 4-symbol codes?
questions.explanation: With repetition allowed, each of 4 positions has 4 choices, giving 4 to the fourth power equals 256. Without repetition the count would be smaller.
questions.hint: Raise the alphabet size to the code length.

questions.learningObjective: Compute permutations of distinct items
questions.stem: A report ranks 6 distinct projects in order; how many possible rankings?
questions.explanation: Six distinct items arranged in order give 6 factorial equals 720. Repetition is impossible because each project appears once.
questions.hint: Multiply 6 times 5 times 4 and so on.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish repetition cases in a mixed problem
questions.stem: A workplace badge has 3 letters from A-Z, letters may repeat; stage one counts with repetition, stage two without.

options.misconception: assumes repetition never changes the count
swaps the repetition and no-repetition results
assumes repetition never helps the count

questions.explanation: With repetition, 26 cubed equals 17576; without, 26 times 25 times 24 equals 15600. Repetition raises the count.
questions.hint: Count repeated choices first, then distinct ones.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations of a subset
questions.stem: A report chooses 3 committee members from 8 staff with no roles; how many committees?

options.text: 3 committees, the size of the subset
options.misconception: returns subset size instead of count
counts ordered arrangements instead of sets
confuses selection count with population size

questions.explanation: Unordered selection uses combinations: 8 choose 3 equals 56. Ordered permutations would overcount by 6.
questions.hint: Use combinations when order of selection does not matter.

questions.learningObjective: Use complement to count avoiding a condition
questions.stem: A workplace survey has 100 respondents; 37 prefer tea; how many do not prefer tea and why use complement?

answer.exemplar: 63 respondents do not prefer tea, because 100 total minus 37 tea-preferring leaves 63; complement avoids listing every non-tea preference.

questions.explanation: Total minus the tea group gives 63 non-tea respondents. Complement is efficient when the unwanted case is large or varied.
questions.hint: Subtract the unwanted count from the total.

questions.topic: Early terms of a recursive sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute early terms from a recurrence
questions.stem: A report defines a_n = 2*a_{n-1}+1 with a_1=2; what is a_4?
questions.explanation: a_2=5, a_3=11, a_4=23. Each term doubles the prior and adds 1, so iterate carefully.

questions.topic: The standard equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: Write the standard equation from center and radius
questions.stem: A blueprint circle has center (2,-3) and radius 5; what is r squared in its standard equation?
questions.explanation: The standard equation uses (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2, so r squared is 5 squared equals 25. The center values become h and k.
questions.hint: Square the radius for the right side.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the product rule to multi-step tasks
questions.stem: A logistics report has 3 warehouses, each with 4 loading docks; how many warehouse-dock pairs?

options.text: 7 pairs, by adding 3 warehouses to 4 docks
options.misconception: adds instead of multiplying independent choices

options.text: 12 pairs, by multiplying 3 warehouses by 4 docks

questions.explanation: Independent choices multiply: 3 times 4 equals 12. Addition would only count one dimension.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the sum rule to alternative routes
questions.stem: A travel report lists 6 highway paths or 4 rail paths, mutually exclusive; a reviewer writes 24 total.

options.text: The reviewer added 6 and 4 to get 10
The reviewer ignored the mutually exclusive condition
The reviewer multiplied 6 and 4, but alternatives add
The reviewer counted only rail paths

questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive alternatives add to 10. Multiplying 6 by 4 would apply to independent sequential choices.

questions.learningObjective: Count repeated-symbol strings
questions.stem: A workplace PIN has 3 digits, each 0-9 with repeats allowed; how many PINs?
questions.explanation: Each of 3 positions has 10 choices, so 10 cubed equals 1000. Repetition makes every position independent.

questions.learningObjective: Count ordered selections without repeats
questions.stem: A report orders 5 distinct speakers at a panel; how many speaking orders?
questions.explanation: Five distinct speakers in order give 5 factorial equals 120. No speaker repeats in a single ordering.

questions.learningObjective: Compare counts in a two-stage problem
questions.stem: A code uses 2 letters from A-Z; stage one allows repeats, stage two forbids them.

options.misconception: swaps the repetition and no-repetition counts
assumes forbidding repeats never lowers count

questions.explanation: With repeats, 26 squared equals 676; without, 26 times 25 equals 650. Forbidding repeats removes 26 cases.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations of a committee
questions.stem: A report selects 2 auditors from 7 staff with no roles; how many auditor pairs?

options.misconception: counts ordered pairs instead of sets
returns subset size instead of count

questions.explanation: Unordered selection gives 7 choose 2 equals 21. Ordered arrangements would double count each pair.

questions.learningObjective: Use complement for a large unwanted set
questions.stem: A department has 80 staff; 29 hold certifications; how many are uncertified and why complement?

answer.exemplar: 51 staff are uncertified, because 80 total minus 29 certified leaves 51; complement is simpler than listing all uncertified roles.

questions.explanation: Subtract certified from total to get 51 uncertified. Complement avoids enumerating many non-certified categories.

questions.topic: Early terms of a recursive sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a linear recurrence
questions.stem: A report defines b_n = 3*b_{n-1}-2 with b_1=4; what is b_3?
questions.explanation: b_2=10, b_3=28. Iterate: 3 times 4 minus 2 equals 10, then 3 times 10 minus 2 equals 28.

questions.topic: The standard equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: Identify radius from standard equation
questions.stem: A blueprint shows (x-1)^2+(y+2)^2=16; what is the radius?

options.text: 16 units, reading r squared as r

questions.explanation: The right side is r squared, so radius is square root of 16 equals 4. Center is (1,-2).
questions.hint: Take the square root of the right side.

questions.learningObjective: Apply product rule to a three-factor task
questions.stem: A report combines 2 sizes, 3 colors, and 2 materials; how many distinct items?
questions.explanation: Three independent factors multiply: 2 times 3 times 2 equals 12. Each combination is distinct.

questions.learningObjective: Apply sum rule to disjoint categories
questions.stem: A survey counts 14 internal and 9 external reviewers, disjoint groups; total reviewers?
questions.explanation: Disjoint groups add: 14 plus 9 equals 23. No overlap means no double counting.

questions.learningObjective: Count repeated-character passwords
questions.stem: A security report says 4-letter passwords from 5 symbols with repeats allowed total 5 times 4 times 3 times 2.

options.text: The report used distinct symbols each time
The report forgot repetition is allowed, so it should be 5 to the fourth
The report added instead of multiplied

questions.explanation: With repetition, each position has 5 choices, giving 5 to the fourth equals 625. The report wrongly forbade repeats.

questions.learningObjective: Count ordered selections of distinct items
questions.stem: A report arranges 4 distinct banners in a row; how many arrangements?

options.misconception: treats arrangement as repeated independent choices

questions.explanation: Four distinct banners in order give 4 factorial equals 24. Repeats are impossible across positions.

questions.learningObjective: Select the correct counting rule
questions.stem: A 3-digit lock code may repeat digits; explain why count is 1000 not 720.

answer.exemplar: The count is 1000 because each of the three positions independently has 10 choices with repetition allowed, giving 10 cubed; 720 would forbid repeats.

questions.explanation: Repetition makes positions independent, so 10 cubed equals 1000. Forbidding repeats would give 10 times 9 times 8 equals 720.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations for a subset
questions.stem: A report chooses 3 features from 10 for a product; how many feature sets?
questions.explanation: Unordered selection gives 10 choose 3 equals 120. Order of features does not matter in a set.

questions.learningObjective: Use complement to count passing outcomes
questions.stem: A test has 50 questions; 12 are flagged difficult; how many are not flagged?
questions.explanation: Total minus flagged gives 38 unflagged. Complement counts the majority without enumerating them.

questions.topic: Early terms of a recursive sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a quadratic recurrence
questions.stem: A report defines c_n = c_{n-1}^2 with c_1=2; stage one c_2, stage two c_3.
questions.explanation: c_2 is 2 squared equals 4, and c_3 is 4 squared equals 16. Squaring accelerates growth.
questions.hint: Square the previous term each stage.

questions.topic: The standard equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: Write full standard equation
questions.stem: A blueprint circle center (3,4) radius 2 is written as (x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=2.

options.text: The center signs should be reversed
The right side should be radius squared, 4
The y term should use x coordinate
The equation needs a plus radius

questions.explanation: Standard form uses r squared on the right, so 2 squared equals 4. Center (3,4) gives (x-3)^2+(y-4)^2.
questions.hint: Square the radius on the right side.

questions.learningObjective: Apply product rule to menu choices
questions.stem: A cafeteria report has 5 mains and 4 sides, choose one of each; how many meals?

options.text: 9 meals, by adding 5 mains to 4 sides
20 meals, by multiplying 5 mains by 4 sides

questions.explanation: Independent choices multiply: 5 times 4 equals 20. Addition would treat them as alternatives.

questions.learningObjective: Apply sum rule to alternative shifts
questions.stem: A schedule has 8 morning or 5 evening shifts, never both; total shifts and why sum?

answer.exemplar: 13 shifts total, because morning and evening are mutually exclusive alternatives, so 8 plus 5 equals 13 rather than multiplying.

questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive alternatives add to 13. Multiplication would apply to independent sequential choices, not alternatives.

questions.learningObjective: Count repeated-digit codes
questions.stem: A report code has 4 digits 0-9 with repeats allowed; how many codes?
questions.explanation: Each of 4 positions has 10 choices, so 10 to the fourth equals 10000. Repetition keeps positions independent.

questions.learningObjective: Count ordered selections without repeats
questions.stem: A report ranks 3 distinct priorities from 6 items; how many rankings?
questions.explanation: Ordered selection of 3 from 6 gives 6 times 5 times 4 equals 120. No item repeats in a ranking.

questions.learningObjective: Compare repetition cases
questions.stem: A 2-letter code from 4 symbols; with repeats allowed versus forbidden, which count is larger?

options.misconception: reverses which case has more codes
assumes forbidding repeats never lowers count

questions.explanation: With repeats, 4 squared equals 16; without, 4 times 3 equals 12. Repeats add the diagonal cases.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations for a team
questions.stem: A report picks 4 team members from 9 staff; a colleague computes 9 times 8 times 7 times 6.

options.text: The colleague added instead of multiplied
The colleague counted ordered teams, not sets
The colleague used the wrong population

questions.explanation: Unordered selection divides ordered count by 4 factorial. The colleague's product counts each team 24 times.
questions.hint: Divide by factorial of team size.

questions.learningObjective: Use complement for a small unwanted set
questions.stem: A batch of 60 items has 4 defective; how many are good using complement?

options.text: 56 good items, by subtracting 4 defective from 60

questions.explanation: Total minus defective gives 56 good items. Complement is efficient when the unwanted set is small.

questions.topic: Early terms of a recursive sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a Fibonacci-like recurrence
questions.stem: A report defines d_n = d_{n-1}+d_{n-2} with d_1=1,d_2=1; what is d_5 and how?

answer.exemplar: d_5 equals 5, computed as d_3=2, d_4=3, d_5=5 by adding the two prior terms each step.

questions.explanation: Fibonacci recurrence gives 1,1,2,3,5. Each term adds the previous two, so d_5 is 5.

questions.topic: The standard equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: Compute radius from equation
questions.stem: A blueprint circle has (x+2)^2+(y-1)^2=9; what is the radius?
questions.explanation: The right side is r squared, so radius is square root of 9 equals 3. Center is (-2,1).

questions.learningObjective: Apply product rule to nested choices
questions.stem: A report has 2 departments, each with 3 teams, each with 4 members; stage one dept-team pairs, stage two full triples.

options.misconception: applies full product to both stages

questions.explanation: Dept-team pairs: 2 times 3 equals 6. Full triples add members: 6 times 4 equals 24.

questions.learningObjective: Apply sum rule to disjoint shifts
questions.stem: A roster has 11 day-shift and 7 night-shift staff, disjoint; total staff?
questions.explanation: Disjoint shifts add: 11 plus 7 equals 18. No staff works both, so no overlap.

questions.learningObjective: Count repeated-symbol strings
questions.stem: A workplace label uses 2 characters from 6 symbols with repeats allowed; how many labels?
questions.explanation: With repeats, each position has 6 choices, so 6 squared equals 36. Forbidding repeats would give 30.

questions.learningObjective: Count ordered selections without repeats
questions.stem: A report orders 3 distinct flags from 5; a colleague writes 5 cubed.

options.text: The colleague added instead of multiplied
The colleague allowed repeats, but flags are distinct
The colleague forgot the order matters

questions.explanation: Distinct ordered selection gives 5 times 4 times 3 equals 60, not 125. Repeats would overcount.

questions.learningObjective: Compare counts in a lock code
questions.stem: A 3-digit lock code forbids repeats; how many codes from digits 0-9?
questions.explanation: Without repeats, 10 times 9 times 8 equals 720. Allowing repeats would give 1000.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations for a subset
questions.stem: A report chooses 2 inspectors from 8 staff; how many inspector pairs?
questions.explanation: Unordered selection gives 8 choose 2 equals 28. Order of inspectors does not matter.

questions.learningObjective: Use complement for a property
questions.stem: A batch of 50 items has 7 defective; stage one good count, stage two defective count.

options.misconception: ignores good count in stage one
ignores defective count in stage two

questions.explanation: Good count is 50 minus 7 equals 43; defective count is 7. Complement gives the majority quickly.
questions.hint: Subtract defective from total for good.

questions.topic: Early terms of a recursive sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of an arithmetic recurrence
questions.stem: A report defines e_n = e_{n-1}+3 with e_1=2; what is e_4?
questions.explanation: e_2=5, e_3=8, e_4=11. Add 3 each step, three steps from e_1.

questions.topic: The standard equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: Identify center from standard equation
questions.stem: A blueprint shows (x-4)^2+(y+1)^2=25; what is the center and why?

answer.exemplar: The center is (4,-1), because standard form (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2 gives h=4 and k=-1 from the signs.

questions.explanation: Standard form has (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2, so h=4 and k=-1. The signs in the equation are opposite the center coordinates.
questions.hint: Read h and k with opposite signs.

questions.learningObjective: Apply product rule to color-size pairs
questions.stem: A product report has 6 colors and 2 sizes; how many color-size variants?
questions.explanation: Independent choices multiply: 6 times 2 equals 12. Each color pairs with each size.

questions.learningObjective: Apply sum rule to alternative suppliers
questions.stem: A procurement report has 9 domestic or 6 foreign suppliers, mutually exclusive; total?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive alternatives add to 15. Multiplication would apply to independent sequential choices.

questions.learningObjective: Count repeated-symbol codes
questions.stem: A workplace code has 5 positions, each any of 3 symbols with repeats; how many codes?
questions.explanation: Each position has 3 choices, so 3 to the fifth equals 243. Repetition keeps positions independent.

questions.learningObjective: Count ordered arrangements of distinct items
questions.stem: A report arranges 4 distinct reports in a stack; how many stacks?
questions.explanation: Four distinct items in order give 4 factorial equals 24. No report repeats in one stack.

questions.learningObjective: Compare counts for a code
questions.stem: A 4-digit code from 0-9 forbids repeats; explain why count is 5040 not 10000.

answer.exemplar: The count is 5040 because forbidding repeats gives 10 times 9 times 8 times 7 equals 5040, while 10000 would allow repeats in every position.

questions.explanation: Without repeats, multiply 10,9,8,7 to get 5040. Allowing repeats would give 10 to the fourth equals 10000.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations for a subset
questions.stem: A report selects 3 reviewers from 10 staff with no roles; how many reviewer groups?

options.misconception: returns subset size instead of count
counts ordered triples instead of sets

questions.explanation: Unordered selection gives 10 choose 3 equals 120. Ordered arrangements would overcount by 6.

questions.learningObjective: Use complement to count non-defective items
questions.stem: A batch of 70 items has 5 defective; a colleague says 70 minus 5 equals 60 good items.

options.text: The colleague should have multiplied 70 by 5
The colleague subtracted correctly but mislabeled 65 as 60
The colleague ignored the defective items
The colleague counted only defective items

questions.explanation: 70 minus 5 equals 65 good items, not 60. The arithmetic subtraction is right but the stated result is wrong.

questions.topic: Early terms of a recursive sequence
questions.learningObjective: Compute terms of a recurrence with subtraction
questions.stem: A report defines f_n = 2*f_{n-1}-1 with f_1=5; what is f_3?
questions.explanation: f_2=9, f_3=17. Iterate: 2 times 5 minus 1 equals 9, then 2 times 9 minus 1 equals 17.

questions.topic: The standard equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: Write center from equation
questions.stem: A blueprint circle has center (-3,2) and radius 4; what is h in the standard equation?
questions.explanation: Standard form uses (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2, so h equals center x-coordinate -3. The equation term is (x+3)^2.

questions.learningObjective: Apply product rule to a three-factor choice
questions.stem: A report combines 3 fonts, 2 sizes, and 2 colors; how many styled text variants?
questions.explanation: Three independent factors multiply: 3 times 2 times 2 equals 12. Addition would treat them as alternatives.

questions.learningObjective: Apply sum rule to alternative plans
questions.stem: A plan offers 13 option A or 8 option B, mutually exclusive; total options?
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive alternatives add: 13 plus 8 equals 21. No option belongs to both groups.

questions.learningObjective: Count repeated-digit PINs
questions.stem: A 4-digit PIN from 0-9; stage one with repeats allowed, stage two without.
questions.explanation: With repeats, 10 to the fourth equals 10000; without, 10 times 9 times 8 times 7 equals 5040.

questions.learningObjective: Count ordered arrangements
questions.stem: A report arranges 5 distinct banners; how many orders and why factorial?

answer.exemplar: There are 120 orders, because each of 5 positions has one fewer choice than the last, giving 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1.

questions.explanation: Five distinct items in order give 5 factorial equals 120. Each position reduces choices by one.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct rule
questions.stem: A license plate has 3 letters and 3 digits, letters and digits may repeat; which rule applies?

options.text: Permutations without repetition for all six
Product rule with repetition in each position
Sum rule across letters and digits

questions.explanation: Each position independently chooses from its alphabet with repeats allowed, so multiply choices per position. Order matters and repetition is allowed.

questions.learningObjective: Compute combinations for a subset
questions.stem: A report chooses 4 features from 12 for a release; how many feature sets?
questions.explanation: Unordered selection gives 12 choose 4 equals 495. Order of features does not matter in a set.
